extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, government officials, regulators, and general readers interested in regulatory reform
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative principles for making government rules and regulatory processes simpler, more user-friendly, and evidence-based. Applies to drafting, oversight, and reform of federal regulatory actions and information-collection requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity as a central goal
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a book about making things simpler. In particular, it is about how governments can be much better, and do much better, if they make people’s lives easier and get rid of unnecessary complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity should be a guiding objective for government design and action; complexity can have its place but should be reduced where it needlessly burdens people. The author uses the analogy of user-friendly computers and tablets—complex machinery made intuitive for users—to argue that government should follow the same principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-friendly design of government processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Government should be a lot more like user-friendly devices: simple, intuitive, not requiring manuals, and usable on the basis of what people already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design rules and procedures so ordinary users can navigate them without specialized knowledge or onerous instructions; prioritize intuitive workflows and interfaces in rule design and public-facing processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act constraint on information collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Paperwork Reduction Act, no federal agency is allowed to collect information from the American people, or to make you fill out a form, unless OIRA allows it to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must obtain OIRA approval before imposing information-collection burdens; the provision serves to limit unnecessary forms and information requests and to force review of collection burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost–benefit requirement for regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory action shall not be undertaken unless the potential benefits to society for the regulation outweigh the potential costs to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA was charged with ensuring compliance with this edict; regulatory decisions should be evaluated by systematic cost–benefit analysis rather than by intuition or political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA oversight of federal regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA (Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs) oversees federal regulation and enforces limits such as the Paperwork Reduction Act and the cost–benefit requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized review by an oversight office is a mechanism to ensure consistency, limit unnecessary burdens, and enforce analytic standards across agencies; such oversight can shepherd simplification initiatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of plain language in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote simplification, including the use of plain language, reductions in red tape, readable summaries of complex rules, and the elimination of costly, unjustified requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft rules and accompanying materials in plain, accessible language; provide readable summaries to increase comprehension and reduce compliance costs for the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction and elimination of unjustified requirements and red tape
rubrics_metrics.description: Elimination of costly, unjustified requirements and reductions in red tape are part of a simplification agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively identify regulatory requirements that impose costs without proportional benefits and remove or streamline them; simplify procedures that create unnecessary burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readable summaries for complex rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide readable summaries of complex rules so the public can understand regulatory obligations without wading through technical legal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summaries should distill key obligations, rights, and compliance steps in clear, nontechnical language to facilitate public understanding and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of low-cost, freedom-preserving 'nudges'
rubrics_metrics.description: Argued in favor of the use of 'nudges'—simple, low-cost, freedom-preserving approaches, drawing directly from behavioral economics, that promise to save money, to improve people’s health, and to lengthen their lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor interventions that preserve choice while steering behavior toward socially desirable outcomes; consider behavioral insights as tools to achieve policy goals with minimal intrusion and expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence-based regulatory decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoted a disciplined emphasis on costs and benefits, in an effort to ensure that the actions of government are based on facts and evidence, not intuitions, anecdotes, dogmas, or the views of powerful interest groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require rigorous empirical analysis and factual grounding for proposed regulations; guard against reliance on anecdotes, intuition, ideological dogma, or concentrated-interest influence when assessing regulatory merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity is compatible with varying government size
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not saying that government should be much smaller... To have a simpler government, you need to have a government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue simplification regardless of whether the overall size of government changes; the goal is clarity and reduced burden, not necessarily smaller institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability of simplification initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiatives designed to increase simplicity can be used not only by governments all over the world but by countless private organizations as well, including businesses large and small, and indeed by all of us in our daily lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider applying the same principles—plain language, reduction of unnecessary steps, user-centered design, evidence-based choices, nudges—to organizational and private-sector processes to realize similar benefits.
